sysd-q-030.title: URL shortening: a short address that redirects
sysd-q-030.text:
Long links are easy to mistype and hard to fit in a message that limits length. URL shortening fixes both. It makes a long URL substantially shorter, yet it still leads to the same page, because a redirect points to the page with the long URL. The browser asks for the short address and gets back a redirect instruction. It carries an HTTP status code such as 301 (moved permanently), 302 (found), 307 (temporary redirect) or 308 (permanent redirect). {{ref:sysd-found-071}} covers those codes.

A short URL saves space when sharing, and it lets links be tracked individually across devices. It helps messaging technologies such as SMS, reduces typing when copying from print, is easier to remember, and can serve as a permalink. Shortening services also give detailed click statistics, which can be simpler than setting up an equally powerful server-side analytics engine and need no access to the server. For security, they typically do not support data: and javascript: URLs, to combat attacks like cross-site scripting and session hijacking.

sysd-q-032.title: What short links cost
sysd-q-032.text: Every short link adds a hop. Short URLs add a layer of complexity to retrieving pages and bring abuse, linkrot and privacy risks. Each access needs at least one more DNS lookup, possibly cached, and one more HTTP or HTTPS request. That adds latency, and a risk of failure if the service becomes unavailable. Linkrot follows from the same dependence: if the service stops working, all URLs it issued become broken. A short URL also hides the target address, so it can redirect to unexpected or malicious sites and bypass site blocklists. Browsers do not resend POST bodies on a redirect, an operational limit of shortening services.

sysd-q-033.title: Short link expiration
sysd-q-033.text: A link that lives forever is not necessarily a good thing. Some providers let a shortened URL expire after a set time, on a certain date, or after a number of uses. Obsolete short URLs stay in circulation long after they stop pointing to a relevant destination, which has security implications. A short-lived URL suits a one-off access or file download that is no longer needed within a couple of minutes. A Microsoft Security Brief recommends short-lived URLs, for security rather than convenience. Providers claiming that short URLs never expire may still discontinue the service. Expiry is a time to live, an idea from {{ref:sysd-blocks-028}}.

sysd-q-034.title: Base62: seven characters, trillions of keys
sysd-q-034.text: Each character added to a short link multiplies the number of possible links by 62. Base62 writes numbers with 62 symbols: the capital letters A-Z, the lower case letters a-z and the digits 0-9. A key of N Base62 characters can name 62^N different URLs. The alphabet suits URLs because the output [a-zA-Z0-9] needs no special characters escaped, while {{ref:sysd-reliab-117}} adds + and / characters that cause issues for URLs. Base62 is also deterministic, with no randomness: one input number or hash always gives the same encoded string.

sysd-q-031.title: Short URL key generation
sysd-q-031.text: Once a service has a long URL, it needs a key to pair with it. A shortening service ties each long URL to a unique key, the part after the domain name, that it builds from letters and digits. Keys can be written in base 36, which is 26 letters and 10 numbers, or in base 62 when upper and lower case differ, as {{ref:sysd-q-034}} describes. Keys are case-sensitive most of the time, so using the wrong case may lead to a different destination URL. A hash function can form the key, or a random number can make the key sequence unpredictable. Users may also propose custom keys.

sysd-q-029.title: Designing a URL shortener
sysd-q-029.text:
The interview question asks for a service that turns a long URL into a short alias and sends visitors back to the original. The service must create a unique short alias for a URL, redirect visitors to the original URL, and expire links after a default timespan. It needs high availability and minimal latency. Preventing abuse and recording analytics are extended requirements.

Start by checking scale assumptions with the interviewer. Assume a read-heavy 100:1 read/write ratio and 100 million links generated per month. That is about 40 URLs per second written and 4000 redirections per second. Taking each request and each stored record as about 500 bytes, incoming bandwidth is 20 KB/second and outgoing is about 2 MB/second. Keeping 12 billion records for 10 years needs around 6 TB. By the 80/20 rule, caching 20% of the 350M redirection requests per day needs around 35GB of memory per day. This is the style of reasoning in {{ref:sysd-found-096}}.

Two tables suffice at first: users (name, email, createdAt) and URLs (expiration, hash, originalURL and the creator's userID), with the hash column indexed. Data that is not strongly relational suits NoSQL such as DynamoDB, Cassandra or MongoDB. The API has three calls. Create URL takes an API key, the original URL and an optional expiration, and returns the short URL. Get URL maps a short URL back to the original. Delete URL returns a boolean result. The API key prevents abuse: it lets the service limit each user to a certain number of requests per second or minute, a standard practice for developer APIs.

The hard part is making the key, as {{ref:sysd-q-031}} describes. Base62 (A-Z, a-z, 0-9) gives about 3.5 trillion 7-character keys (62^7), and MD5 hashing the URL yields 32 hex digits to make one. Both risk duplicates and collisions, and recomputing hashes adds overhead. A counter encoded in base62 is a single point of failure, and several counters collide. ZooKeeper can hand each server a range such as 1 to 1,000,000, which guarantees non-duplicate keys, and it can itself run in several instances. The alternative is a standalone Key Generation Service that creates unique keys ahead of time in a separate database. Used keys move to another table under locking, so concurrent servers never share one, and some keys are kept in memory.

To create a URL, the API server gets a unique key from the Key Generation Service, which marks it used. The server writes the entry to the database and cache and returns HTTP 201 (Created). To access a URL, the API server checks the cache first and falls back to the database. It then issues an HTTP 301 (Redirect) to the original URL, or sends HTTP 404 (Not found) if the key is missing. The redirect works as {{ref:sysd-found-071}} explains.

To scale out the database, partition it horizontally by hash, list, range or composite schemes, as {{ref:sysd-scale-087}} describes. These can still distribute data and load unevenly, and consistent hashing fixes that; see {{ref:sysd-scale-078}}. Redis or Memcached servers beside the API server cache 20% of daily traffic, as {{ref:sysd-blocks-001}} describes. They use Least Recently Used eviction, which discards the least recently used key first. On a cache miss they read the database and update the cache. Expired links can be removed in two ways. Active cleanup is a lightweight cron-like service that periodically deletes them from storage and cache. Passive cleanup is a lazy removal when a user accesses an expired link.

To remove single points of failure, run multiple instances of the servers and the Key Generation Service. Put load balancers between components, add read replicas for the database, a standby replica for the key database, and a replicated cache. The thing to remember is the shape. It is a read-heavy lookup, where a cache serves the hot links and a Key Generation Service makes sure no two links share a key.

sysd-q-063.title: Pastebin
sysd-q-063.text: Chatrooms gave pastebins their purpose. Sending large blocks of computer data there disrupts closely interleaved conversation, so users are told to paste elsewhere and share the link. A pastebin is an online content-hosting service where users store plain text, such as source code snippets or error logs, and share it by link. Each stored text entry is commonly called a paste, and account holders can typically edit or delete their pastes at any time. Accounts let users manage and organize their content, and many platforms let users set a paste as public or private. Pastebins may add features such as commenting, rendering markup like Markdown or ReStructuredText, or version control. Designing one is like designing a URL shortener, as {{ref:sysd-q-031}} sets it up, except that the service stores the paste contents instead of the original unshortened URL.

sysd-q-062.title: Designing Pastebin
sysd-q-062.text:
The interview question asks for a service where a user enters text and gets a random link, then views the paste by its URL. Pastes do not expire by default but may have a timed expiration. The service tracks monthly visits, deletes expired pastes and stays available. Out of scope are registering an account, verifying email, logging in, editing the document, setting visibility and letting the user choose the shortlink.

Traffic is not evenly distributed, pastes are text only and analytics need not be realtime. Assume 10 million paste writes and 100 million reads per month, a 10:1 ratio, which is 4 writes and 40 reads per second on average. Each paste is about 1.27 KB: 1 KB of content, a 7-byte shortlink, a 4-byte expiration, a 5-byte created_at and a 255-byte paste_path. That means 12.7 GB of new content per month and about 450 GB in 3 years.

A relational database can act as a large hash table that maps the generated url to a file server and path. Instead of a file server, use a managed object store such as Amazon S3, or a NoSQL document store. {{ref:sysd-blocks-145}} covers object stores. A NoSQL key-value store is another alternative to the relational hash table, and a good answer discusses the trade-offs between SQL and NoSQL. In the pastes table, a primary key on the shortlink column creates an index that enforces uniqueness. An extra index on created_at speeds lookups to log time instead of a full table scan, as {{ref:sysd-blocks-084}} explains.

To generate the unique url, take the MD5 hash of the user's ip_address plus timestamp, or of random data. Base 62 encode it and keep the first 7 characters. The 62^7 values suffice for 360 million shortlinks in 3 years. Base 62 encodes to [a-zA-Z0-9], which suits urls without escaping special characters, and it is deterministic. Base 64 is another popular encoding, but its additional + and / characters cause issues for urls.

To create a paste, the Web Server, a reverse proxy, forwards the request to the Write API server. That server generates a unique url, regenerates on a duplicate, saves to the SQL pastes table and the Object Store, and returns the url. To view a paste, the Web Server forwards the request to the Read API server. It checks the SQL Database for the url, fetches the contents from the Object Store if found, and otherwise returns an error message. Clients use a public REST API, and internal communications could use Remote Procedure Calls.

Because realtime analytics are not required, MapReduce the Web Server logs to get hit counts. The Analytics Database could be a data warehouse such as Amazon Redshift or Google BigQuery. To delete expired pastes, scan the SQL Database for entries whose expiration timestamp is older than the current timestamp. Delete them or mark them as expired, as {{ref:sysd-q-033}} discusses.

Do not jump straight to the final design. State that scaling is iterative: benchmark and load test, profile for bottlenecks, address them while weighing alternatives and trade-offs, and repeat. In the scaled design, an object store like S3 handles 12.7 GB of new content per month. A memory cache serves popular content for the 40 average reads per second and traffic spikes. SQL read replicas handle the cache misses. See {{ref:sysd-blocks-001}} and {{ref:sysd-scale-049}}.

openers.q: The rest of the course is a set of design questions, the kind an interviewer asks and a good answer takes apart piece by piece. The first is a URL shortener, which must create a unique short alias for a URL, redirect visitors to the original, and stay available with minimal latency. A pastebin stores plain text such as source code snippets or error logs and shares it by link, which makes it a close cousin. After that comes instant messaging, which sends messages in real time between two or more parties, and which can be built so that only the sender and the intended recipients can read them. Each question gathers the ideas it needs before it walks through a full answer.
openers.authentication-and-security: Every request that reaches a system raises two questions: who is asking, and what may they do. This chapter takes both in turn. It starts with authentication, the act of proving an assertion such as a user's identity, and the three kinds of evidence behind it: something the user knows, has or is. It then turns to authorization, which specifies rights to access resources, and to OAuth 2.0, which lets a user grant an application consented access to another site without sharing credentials. Along the way come the attacks that shape the defenses, such as cross-site scripting, and the details that matter, such as the random data called a salt that goes into password hashing.
openers.design-a-url-shortener: A short link does one job: it makes a long URL substantially shorter while it still leads to the same page, through a redirect. That convenience has costs, because short URLs add a layer of complexity to retrieving pages and bring abuse, linkrot (links that stop working) and privacy risks. This chapter looks at how a shortening service ties each long URL to a unique key built from letters and digits, and at Base62, which writes numbers with 62 symbols. It also covers why some providers let links expire after a set time, on a certain date, or after a number of uses. It ends with a full design that must create unique aliases, redirect visitors and stay highly available with minimal latency.
openers.design-pastebin: A pastebin is an online content-hosting service where users store plain text, such as source code snippets or error logs, and share it by link. In the design question, a user enters text and gets a random link, then views the paste by its URL. Pastes do not expire by default but may have a timed expiration, and the service tracks monthly visits, deletes expired pastes and stays available. A reader who has just met the URL shortener will find the problem familiar.

reviews.authentication-and-security: Authentication proves who is asking, through something the user knows, has or is. Several factors together are harder to fake than one, though even multi-factor schemes can be phished or bypassed. Passwords are kept as salted hashes, made deliberately slow by functions such as bcrypt and Argon2, so a stolen database is hard to crack. Once identity is settled, authorization decides what that user may do, guided by least privilege and, under zero trust, checked on every request. Tokens carry that decision across the web, from OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect to signed JSON Web Tokens, while single sign-on trades one convenient login for a bigger target.
reviews.design-a-url-shortener: A shortener is a redirect plus a key. The key is built from letters and digits, often in Base62, and the design has to produce it without collisions at the scale the estimates set. Short links bring their own costs, from added latency and linkrot to hidden destinations, which is one reason expiration is worth designing in. In the full design, a Key Generation Service hands out keys, a cache and a sharded database serve the redirects, and replicas remove single points of failure.
reviews.design-pastebin: Pastebin takes the shortener's idea and changes what sits behind the key: the service stores the paste contents instead of the original unshortened URL. The design pairs a database that maps each generated url to the contents with an object store that holds them, and it deletes expired pastes by scanning for old timestamps. The average load is modest, 4 writes and 40 reads per second, so a memory cache and read replicas carry it. Throughout, the answer treats scaling as iterative: benchmark, find the bottleneck, weigh alternatives, and repeat.
